answer_text:
Let \(X\sim N(0,1)\). Then

\[
\psi(\lambda)=\mathbb{E}\left[\Phi(\lambda X)^K\right].
\]

First, \(\psi\) is even:

\[
\psi(-\lambda)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\Phi(-\lambda x)^K\phi(x)\,dx
=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\Phi(\lambda x)^K\phi(x)\,dx=\psi(\lambda).
\]

For \(K>0\), differentiate under the integral sign:

\[
\psi'(\lambda)
=K\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x\,\phi(\lambda x)\,\Phi(\lambda x)^{K-1}\phi(x)\,dx.
\]

For \(\lambda>0\), pair the terms \(x\) and \(-x\):

\[
\psi'(\lambda)
=
K\int_0^\infty x\,\phi(\lambda x)\phi(x)
\left[
\Phi(\lambda x)^{K-1}-\Phi(-\lambda x)^{K-1}
\right]dx.
\]

Let \(t=\Phi(\lambda x)\in(1/2,1)\). Then \(\Phi(-\lambda x)=1-t\). The sign of the bracket is the sign of

\[
t^{K-1}-(1-t)^{K-1}.
\]

Thus,

- if \(K>1\), then \(\psi'(\lambda)>0\) for \(\lambda>0\);
- if \(K=1\), then \(\psi'(\lambda)=0\) for all \(\lambda\);
- if \(0<K<1\), then \(\psi'(\lambda)<0\) for \(\lambda>0\).

Also,

\[
\psi(0)=\left(\frac12\right)^K=2^{-K},
\]

and by dominated convergence,

\[
\lim_{|\lambda|\to\infty}\psi(\lambda)=\frac12.
\]

Therefore, over \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\),

\[
\boxed{
\begin{cases}
K>1: & \lambda=0 \text{ is the unique global minimizer; no finite maximizer exists, since } \sup_\lambda \psi(\lambda)=\frac12.\\[2mm]
0<K<1: & \lambda=0 \text{ is the unique global maximizer; no finite minimizer exists, since } \inf_\lambda \psi(\lambda)=\frac12.\\[2mm]
K=1: & \psi(\lambda)\equiv \frac12, \text{ so every }\lambda\text{ is both a maximizer and minimizer.}
\end{cases}
}
\]

In the common case where \(K\) is a positive integer with \(K\ge 2\), the answer is: \(\boxed{\lambda=0}\) is the unique minimizer, and the supremum is approached only as \(|\lambda|\to\infty\).
